Models

Models.Rmd

This vignette describes the two latent variable models implemented in lblvm: the bounded-continuous response model and the discretized response model (DRM). Both models use the same logit-beta framework, but differ in how the response is observed.

Figure 1 Bounded-continuous response model in Panel (a) and discretized response model in Panel (b). The black solid lines in the two panels are identical and are the μ\mu-curves. The grey curves represent the probability densities of continuous item responses in Panel (a) and those of internal judgment continuum in Panel (b). The grey line segments, located exactly on the μ\mu-curve, indicate the means of the densities. The relative width of the color bands in Panel (b) can be estimated in the discretized response model.

Bounded-continuous response model

The bounded-continuous response model is designed for responses that take values between 0 and 1. Let xijx_{ij} denote the response of person ii to item jj, and let θi\theta_i denote the person’s latent trait. The expected response is modeled as

logit⁡(μij)=ajθi+cj, \operatorname{logit}(\mu_{ij}) = a_j\theta_i+c_j,

where

μij=E(xij∣θi)=exp⁡(ajθi+cj)1+exp⁡(ajθi+cj). \mu_{ij} = E(x_{ij}\mid\theta_i) = \frac{\exp(a_j\theta_i+c_j)} {1+\exp(a_j\theta_i+c_j)}.

Here, aja_j is the item slope and cjc_j is the item intercept. The slope determines how rapidly the expected response changes as the latent trait changes, whereas the intercept determines the location of the expected response curve. The latent trait can be multidimensional, and in such cases, aa and θ\theta become DD-dimensional vectors and ajθia_j\theta_i in the above equation is substituted with an inner product 𝐚j⋅𝛉i=∑d=1Dajdθid\mathbf{a}_j\cdot\mathbf{\theta}_i=\sum_{d=1}^{D}a_{jd}\theta_{id}.

The response is then assumed to follow a beta distribution,

xij∣θi∼Beta⁡(μijνj,(1−μij)νj), x_{ij}\mid\theta_i \sim \operatorname{Beta} \left( \mu_{ij}\nu_j, (1-\mu_{ij})\nu_j \right),

where νj>0\nu_j>0 is an item-specific precision parameter. Under this parameterization,

Var⁡(xij∣θi)=μij(1−μij)νj+1. \operatorname{Var}(x_{ij}\mid\theta_i) = \frac{\mu_{ij}(1-\mu_{ij})}{\nu_j+1}.

The precision parameter controls how concentrated the responses are around their expected value. Larger values of νj\nu_j correspond to greater precision and, therefore, less residual variation.

The bounded-continuous model can therefore be understood in two parts. The logit equation describes the relationship between the latent trait and the expected response, while the beta distribution describes how individual responses vary around that expectation.

Discretized response model

The discretized response model (DRM) extends the bounded-continuous model to ordered categorical responses. The key assumption is that an ordered categorical response arises by discretizing an underlying bounded-continuous judgment.

For example, consider an item with five response categories:

Strongly disagree | Disagree | Neutral | Agree | Strongly agree

DRM assumes that these categories correspond to five consecutive intervals on an underlying continuum from 0 to 1. Let the boundaries of these intervals be

0=T0<T1<T2<T3<T4<T5=1. 0=T_0<T_1<T_2<T_3<T_4<T_5=1.

The underlying continuous response follows the same beta distribution as the bounded-continuous model. Therefore, for category zz, the probability of observing that category is the probability that the underlying response falls within its corresponding interval:

P(Uij=z∣θi)=∫Tz−1TzBeta⁡(x∣μijνj,(1−μij)νj)dx, P(U_{ij}=z\mid\theta_i) = \int_{T_{z-1}}^{T_z} \operatorname{Beta} \left(x \mid \mu_{ij}\nu_j, (1-\mu_{ij})\nu_j \right)\,dx,

where Beta⁡(x∣μijνj,(1−μij)νj)\operatorname{Beta}\left(x \mid \mu_{ij}\nu_j,(1-\mu_{ij})\nu_j\right) is the beta density implied by the bounded-continuous model.

For example, the probability of the fourth category is

P(Uij=4∣θi)=∫T3T4Beta⁡(x∣μijνj,(1−μij)νj)dx. P(U_{ij}=4\mid\theta_i) = \int_{T_3}^{T_4} \operatorname{Beta} \left(x \mid \mu_{ij}\nu_j, (1-\mu_{ij})\nu_j \right)\,dx.

Thus, the probability of a category is determined by both the underlying judgment distribution and the interval assigned to that category.

Relationship between the two models

The two models share the same underlying logit-beta response process. Their difference is the observation mechanism.

For the bounded-continuous response model, the underlying response is observed directly:

θi→μij→xij. \theta_i \longrightarrow \mu_{ij} \longrightarrow x_{ij}.

For DRM, the same underlying response is discretized into ordered categories:

θi→μij→xij→Uij. \theta_i \longrightarrow \mu_{ij} \longrightarrow x_{ij} \longrightarrow U_{ij}.

The first two stages are identical. The difference is that DRM introduces thresholds that divide the bounded continuum into intervals, and the observed category indicates which interval contains the underlying judgment.

Consequently, DRM allows the latent-trait effects and the response categorization process to be represented separately: the latent trait determines the location and precision of the underlying judgment distribution, while the thresholds determine how that judgment is translated into an ordered response.
